prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that periodically reads moisture levels from a DFRobot Soil Moisture Sensor v2.0 (analog resistive) using an MCP3008 ADC connected on the SPI0 hardware bus, with CE0 on GPIO8 (BCM), MOSI on GPIO10 (BCM), MISO on GPIO9 (BCM), and SCLK on GPIO11 (BCM); the sensor’s analog output is wired to MCP3008 channel 0 (CH0), and the program must sample once per second, logging the raw 10‑bit ADC value (0‑1023) to the console together with a timestamp, while providing robust error handling for any SPI initialization or transfer failures, ensuring that the SPI handle is closed and the driver library is terminated cleanly on all exit paths, and supporting graceful shutdown when receiving SIGINT or SIGTERM.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that interfaces the AZDelivery KY-026 Flame Sensor Module and an MCP3008 ADC over SPI0 running at 1 MHz, reading the digital output D0 of the flame sensor on GPIO4 (BCM) and routing the analog output A0 to MCP3008 channel 0 (single‑ended) while using the MCP3008 chip‑enable CE0 on GPIO8 (BCM); the program must initialize the driver, verify successful SPI open and transfer operations, and on each one‑second interval log a timestamped CSV row containing the current time, a boolean flame‑detected flag derived from the digital line, and an approximated temperature calculated from the analog reading to a file named flame_data.csv, while handling errors by skipping the entry and printing a diagnostic message if the sensor is absent or any SPI or file operation fails, and must ensure all resources are cleanly released on normal exit or when a SIGINT is received.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously monitors a Keyes KY-026 Flame Sensor connected to GPIO4 (BCM) as a digital input and an LM393‑based Heat Sensor whose analog output is read through an ADS1115 on I2C bus 1 using channel AIN0 (single‑ended), polling both every 100 ms with a 50 ms debounce applied to the flame sensor, and activates an active‑HIGH buzzer on GPIO27 (BCM) for exactly 2 seconds when both sensors indicate a fire condition at the same time; the program must log a fire event with a timestamp to a file named fire_log.txt when both conditions trigger, log “Flame detected!” if only the flame sensor is active, and log the temperature reading if only the temperature exceeds 60 °C, while performing thorough error handling that checks driver library initialization, I2C opening, ADC configuration writes, ADC reads, and log file creation, printing descriptive error messages to stderr for any failure, releasing any resources acquired so far and exiting with code 1 on any initialization error, and, if an ADC read fails due to I2C error or missing sensor, logging the error and continuing without crashing; the application should handle SIGINT by clearing a running flag so the main loop exits cleanly, and on exit it must turn off the buzzer, deregister any interrupt service routine, close the I2C handle, close the log file, and invoke the driver library’s cleanup call, using only the provided driver library (no other libraries), driving the buzzer with a simple digital write (no PWM), and compiling without warnings under gcc ‑Wall with no undeclared identifiers or implicit declarations.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads the analog output of a YL‑83 rain sensor through an MCP3008 ADC connected on SPI0 using chip‑enable CE0 (bus 0, channel 0) in SPI mode 0 at 1 MHz, sampling once per second; the MCP3008 must be accessed in single‑ended mode on channel 0 with VDD = 3.3 V giving a full‑scale ADC value of 1023, and each sample should be mapped to a rainfall intensity level, then logged to stdout with a timestamp, the raw ADC value, and the computed intensity; the program must verify successful initialization of the driver, opening of the SPI device, and every subsequent API call, and if any SPI transfer fails it must print an error message and skip that reading, retrying on the next cycle rather than using stale data; finally, it must handle SIGINT (Ctrl‑C) to perform a graceful shutdown by closing the SPI handle and terminating the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that reads a potentiometer connected to an MCP3008 ADC via the SPI0 bus using CE0 on GPIO8 (BCM) at 1 MHz, mode 0, channel 0, and uses the sampled value to set the speed of a motor driven by PWM on GPIO18 (BCM) with a 1 kHz frequency and a duty‑cycle range of 0‑1023, performing an ADC read and PWM update every 100 ms, printing both the raw ADC reading and the resulting PWM value to stdout, while checking that the SPI interface is successfully initialized, verifying the SPI handle, inspecting the result of each SPI transfer and gracefully handling any transient SPI errors without crashing, and installing a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that stops the PWM output and releases all resources before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously monitors a Honeywell SS49E linear Hall‑effect sensor through an ADS1115 ADC on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, configured for a single‑ended input on AIN0 with a PGA gain of 4.096 V, and prints the magnetic field strength in Gauss to the console every 100 ms; the program must also accept a user‑configurable threshold in Gauss via a “‑t” command‑line argument (default 100.0 Gauss) and, when the measured field exceeds this threshold, blink an LED connected to GPIO17 (BCM) with a 50 ms on / 50 ms off duty cycle for a total of 1 second, while validating the driver and I2C initialization, checking every I2C read and handling any ADC communication failures gracefully; finally, the application must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, turning the LED off and terminating the driver usage properly.

```
gcc -Wall -Wextra -Werror -std=c99 -pedantic -o soil_moisture soil_moisture.c -lwiringPi
```

sudo ./soil_moisture

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that opens the USB camera on /dev/video0 in blocking mode (O_RDWR without O_NONBLOCK), queries the device capabilities to ensure both V4L2_CAP_VIDEO_CAPTURE and V4L2_CAP_STREAMING are present, sets the pixel format to V4L2_PIX_FMT_MJPEG with a width of 192 (the documented value) and V4L2_FIELD_NONE, requests four MMAP buffers, starts streaming, dequeues a single frame, verifies that the dequeued buffer’s bytesused field is greater than zero, and writes the raw MJPEG bytes directly to a file named image.jpg without any re‑encoding; every ioctl, open, mmap, and fopen call must have its return value checked and any failure reported with a descriptive perror/errno message, and a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler must be installed to stop streaming, unmap all buffers, free the buffer array, close the file and the device file descriptor on all exit paths, ensuring clean resource release.
raw:
```
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <errno.h>
#include <fcntl.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <sys/ioctl.h>
#include <sys/mman.h>
#include <linux/videodev2.h>

#define CLEAR(x) memset(&(x), 0, sizeof(x))

int main(int argc, char **argv)
{
    int fd;
    struct v4l2_capability cap;
    struct v4l2_format fmt;
    struct v4l2_requestbuffers req;
    struct v4l2_buffer buf;
    unsigned char *start;
    int n_buffers;
    int type;
    int i;

    fd = open("/dev/video0", O_RDWR);
    if (fd < 0) {
        perror("open");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    if (ioctl(fd, VIDIOC_QUERYCAP, &cap) < 0) {
        perror("VIDIOC_QUERYCAP");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    if (!(cap.capabilities & V4L2_CAP_VIDEO_CAPTURE)) {
        fprintf(stderr, "The device does not support video capture\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    if (!(cap.capabilities & V4L2_CAP_STREAMING)) {
        fprintf(stderr, "The device does not support streaming\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    CLEAR(fmt);
    fmt.type = V4L2_BUF_TYPE_VIDEO_CAPTURE;
    fmt.fmt.pix.width = 192;
    fmt.fmt.pix.height = 108;
    fmt.fmt.pix.pixelformat = V4L2_PIX_FMT_MJPEG;
    fmt.fmt.pix.field = V4L2_FIELD_NONE;

    if (ioctl(fd, VIDIOC_S_FMT, &fmt) < 0) {
        perror("VIDIOC_S_FMT");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    CLEAR(req);
    req.count = 4;
    req.type = V4L2_BUF_TYPE_VIDEO_CAPTURE;
    req.memory = V4L2_MEMORY_MMAP;

    if (ioctl(fd, VIDIOC_REQBUFS, &req) < 0) {
        perror("VIDIOC_REQBUFS");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    n_buffers = req.count;

    start = malloc(n_buffers * sizeof(*start));
    if (!start) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    for (i = 0; i < n_buffers; ++i) {
        CLEAR(buf);
        buf.type = V4L2_BUF_TYPE_VIDEO_CAPTURE;
        buf.memory = V4L2_MEMORY_MMAP;
        buf.index = i;

        if (ioctl(fd, VIDIOC_QUERYBUF, &buf) < 0) {
            perror("VIDIOC_QUERYBUF");
            exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
        }

        start[i] = mmap(NULL, buf.length, PROT_READ | PROT_WRITE, MAP_SHARED, fd, buf.m.offset);
        if (start[i] == MAP_FAILED) {
            perror("mmap");
            exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
        }
    }

    type = V4L2_BUF_TYPE_VIDEO_CAPTURE;
    if (ioctl(fd, VIDIOC_STREAMON, &type) < 0) {
        perror("VIDIOC_STREAMON");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    CLEAR(buf);
    buf.type = V4L2_BUF_TYPE_VIDEO_CAPTURE;
    buf.memory = V4L2_MEMORY_MMAP;

    if (ioctl(fd, VIDIOC_DQBUF, &buf) < 0) {
        perror("VIDIOC_DQBUF");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    if (buf.bytesused == 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "No data\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    FILE *fp = fopen("image.jpg", "wb");
    if (!fp) {
        perror("fopen");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    fwrite(start[buf.index], buf.bytesused, 1, fp);
    fclose(fp);

    type = V4L2_BUF_TYPE_VIDEO_CAPTURE;
    if (ioctl(fd, VIDIOC_STREAMOFF, &type) < 0) {
        perror("VIDIOC_STREAMOFF");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    for (i = 0; i < n_buffers; ++i) {
        if (munmap(start[i], buf.length) < 0) {
            perror("munmap");
            exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
        }
    }

    free(start);
    close(fd);
    exit(EXIT_SUCCESS);
}

The program opens the device file descriptor for /dev/video0 with O_RDWR and checks that VIDIOC_QUERYCAP returns V4L2_CAP_VIDEO_CAPTURE and V4L2_CAP_STREAMING are set. VIDIOC_S_FMT is then used to set the width and height to 192 and the pixel format to V4L2_PIX_FMT_MJPEG and V4L2_FIELD_NONE (no interlacing). VIDIOC_REQBUFS is then used to request four MMAP buffers. VIDIOC_STREAMON is then used to start streaming. VIDIOC_DQBUF is then used to dequeue a single frame. VIDIOC_STREAMOFF is then used to stop streaming. MMAP buffers are then unmapped and the device file descriptor is closed.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that creates a wave‑like animation on an 8x8 common‑anode LED matrix driven directly over GPIO, with the row anodes connected to GPIO 2, 3, 4, 17, 27, 22, 10, 9 (BCM) and the column cathodes to GPIO 14, 15, 18, 23, 24, 25, 8, 7 (BCM); the program must scan the columns left to right, clearing the matrix before each column by setting all column cathodes HIGH and all row anodes LOW, then for each column set the column cathode LOW and light the LEDs sequentially by setting the corresponding row anodes HIGH, observing a 150 ms delay between columns, checking the result of every GPIO operation and handling a chip‑open failure, using the driver library v2 API for all GPIO calls, and installing a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM that cleanly releases all GPIO lines on exit, while respecting the hardware constraint that each column cathode is wired through a current‑limiting resistor (e.g., 220 Ω) and that a column lights when its cathode is LOW and all row anodes are HIGH, and the program should run indefinitely until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously reads distance measurements for multiple targets from an STMicroelectronics VL53L3CX Time‑of‑Flight multi‑target sensor connected on I2C bus 1, polling the sensor every 100 ms and printing to the console ISO‑8601 timestamped distance values for all detected targets; the program must verify the sensor model ID during initialization, perform the required complex proprietary initialization sequence (or clearly stub the proprietary firmware download with a descriptive comment while keeping the I2C communication and error handling fully implemented), check every I2C read/write return code and handle sensor‑absent and bus‑error conditions, and ensure that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path, including a graceful shutdown when receiving SIGINT.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads distance data from a Melexis MLX75031 Time‑of‑Flight sensor on I2C bus 1, samples the sensor every 100 ms, and appends each reading to a file named depth_log.csv, creating a CSV header row if the file is newly created and writing timestamped distance values; the program must verify successful initialization of the sensor interface, opening of the I2C bus, each I2C read/write transaction, and all file operations, and if an I2C read fails it must log a row with distance ‑1, attempt to re‑open the I2C handle, and continue sampling, while also handling SIGINT to perform a graceful shutdown that closes the I2C handle, closes the log file, and terminates the sensor interface without using any driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously reads proximity and ambient‑light data from a Silicon Labs Si1145 proximity/ambient‑light sensor attached to I2C bus 1, sampling every 500 ms, and appends each reading to a file named biometric_log.txt prefixed with an ISO‑8601 timestamp; the program must handle I2C read failures gracefully by logging the error and continuing, and if the sensor is absent or initialization fails it must print a diagnostic message to stderr and exit with a non‑zero status, while also installing a SIGINT handler that, upon receipt, cleanly closes the I2C handle, flushes and closes the log file, and calls the sensor’s library API call() before terminating.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that continuously polls an E18‑D50NK IR proximity sensor connected to GPIO line 4 (BCM, physical pin 7) every 100 ms, reads the sensor which drives the line LOW when an object is within the calibrated range and HIGH otherwise, and detects the falling edge from HIGH to LOW so that a timestamped entry is written only once per detection to a file named proximity.log using an ISO 8601 UTC format such as “2024-01-15T12:34:56Z Object detected”; when a detection occurs the program must also blink an LED attached to GPIO line 17 (BCM, physical pin 11) by turning it on for 100 ms and then off, and it must check the return status of every driver call, handle any file‑I/O errors, and on any exit path—including receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM—release the GPIO lines and close the chip, opening the GPIO chip first with the library’s API call that takes the default chip name and, if that fails, falling back to the library’s API call with the string “the library’s API call”, never invoking the API without arguments.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads proximity and ambient light data from a Silicon Labs Si1145 sensor attached to I2C bus 1, first verifying the sensor’s PART_ID before entering an infinite loop that samples the two measurements once per second, and logs each reading to a file named biometric_data.log in CSV format with an ISO‑8601 timestamp followed by the proximity value and the ambient light value, flushing the file after every write; the program must check the return code of every I2C read and write operation, handle cases where the sensor is absent or the bus reports errors in a graceful manner, and install a SIGINT handler that, upon termination, closes the I2C handle, closes the log file, and calls the sensor’s API call() function for proper cleanup.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that drives an HC‑SR04 ultrasonic sensor over GPIO, using GPIO 17 (BCM) as the TRIGGER output and GPIO 27 (BCM) as the ECHO input, with a 1 kΩ/2 kΩ voltage divider on the echo line to protect the 3.3 V‑tolerant pins from the sensor’s 5 V logic; the program must issue a 10 µs trigger pulse, then wait up to 30 ms for the echo rise and up to another 30 ms for the echo pulse width, compute the distance, reject any reading outside the 2‑400 cm range, and every 60 seconds log the result to a file named distance_log.txt with an ISO‑8601 timestamp, including explicit error or timeout entries, and if the measured distance is below 15 cm also log the message “Time to water the plant!”; all driver calls must be checked for failure, handling the sensor‑absent case where the echo never rises and the timeout case where the echo stays high, and the application must catch SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that releases all resources and closes the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the Adafruit APDS9960 sensor on I2C bus 1 to poll the device every 100 ms, detect proximity events and read the raw RGB color values, and whenever the proximity reading exceeds the threshold of 200 it appends a line containing the timestamp, the three RGB components and the proximity value to a CSV file named color_proximity_log.csv; the program must handle I2C communication errors by closing and reopening the bus and re‑initializing the sensor, and it must also catch SIGINT and SIGTERM signals to perform a graceful shutdown that closes the I2C handle, finalizes the CSV file, and releases any resources allocated by the driver.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses two TCRT5000 IR reflective sensors connected to the GPIO bus, with sensor 1 wired to GPIO 17 (BCM) and sensor 2 to GPIO 18 (BCM), to detect object proximity and log the binary readings (0 or 1) together with timestamps every 100 milliseconds to a file named obstacle_log.txt; the program must include robust error handling for any GPIO setup failures, and if a sensor read fails it should write an error message to stderr while continuing operation, and it must also handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) to perform a graceful shutdown that releases all resources before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously reads the distance from a TDK InvenSense ICU‑20201 ultrasonic Time‑of‑Flight sensor on I2C bus 1, sampling every 100 ms, and drives an LED connected to GPIO 17 (BCM numbering) such that the LED is turned on when the measured distance is below 20 cm and off otherwise, while logging each distance reading together with an ISO‑8601 timestamp to a file named distance_log.txt; the implementation must check the result of every I2C, driver library, and file operation, handle cases where the sensor is absent or the bus reports errors in a graceful manner, and ensure that all resources—including the I2C handle, the GPIO pin, and any driver state—are cleanly released on every exit path by handling SIGINT and SIGTERM signals.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously reads proximity and ambient light data from a Silicon Labs Si1182‑GMR Optical Proximity and Ambient Light Sensor on I2C bus 1, sampling both measurements every 500 ms, and appends each reading with a timestamp to a file named biometric_log.txt; the implementation must check the return value of every I2C read and write operation, retry any failed read up to three times, and gracefully handle cases where the sensor is absent or the bus reports errors, while also installing a SIGINT (Ctrl+C) handler that cleanly releases the I2C handle, closes the log file, and terminates any driver resources before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads distance measurements from a TDK InvenSense ICU-20201 ultrasonic Time‑of‑Flight sensor on I2C bus 1 at a 50 ms polling interval, lights an LED connected to GPIO 17 (BCM) whenever the measured distance falls below a configurable threshold (default 100 mm, supplied as the first command‑line argument), logs each reading with a timestamp to a file named “tof_log.txt”, verifies the sensor’s WHO_AM_I register during initialization, checks all I2C read/write return codes, gracefully handles sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions without crashing, and ensures that on any exit path—including receipt of SIGINT—the program releases the I2C handle, resets the GPIO, and performs any required driver cleanup.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that communicates with an Omron B5L‑LD50‑07050 3D TOF sensor over the I2C bus (/dev/i2c-1) to detect intrusion events within 1 meter and log the average distance; the program must send the documented 4‑byte command frame to request a measurement, wait at least 10 ms before reading the documented 15‑byte response, verify that byte 0 matches the documented header value, extract the 16‑bit big‑endian distance from bytes 11 and 12, sample the sensor ten times per cycle with a 100 ms delay between cycles, compute the average distance, and when the average is less than 1000 mm write a timestamp and the average distance to a file named intrusion_log.txt; all I2C open, ioctl, read and write calls must be checked for failure, and the code must gracefully handle sensor‑absent (I2C NACK) and bus‑error conditions, while also installing a SIGINT handler so that pressing Ctrl‑C closes the I2C file descriptor and any open log files and releases all resources on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the I2C bus 1 to periodically read the distance from an Adafruit VL53L0X Time‑of‑Flight sensor, verifying the sensor’s presence at startup by reading its model ID register and confirming it matches the documented value, and exiting cleanly with an error message if the read fails or the ID mismatches; after successful initialization the program must poll the RESULT_INTERRUPT_STATUS with roughly a 100 ms timeout, obtain a distance measurement, and every 500 ms print to stdout a line formatted as “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS Distance: <N> mm”, while checking every I2C call for errors and printing strerror(errno) on failure, issuing a warning to stderr and continuing to the next iteration for any read/write error that occurs during the loop; the program must also handle SIGINT and SIGTERM gracefully by closing the I2C handle, invoking the library’s cleanup call, and exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that periodically reads the 16‑bit proximity data from a Silicon Labs Si1182 optical sensor connected on I2C bus 1 (GPIO2 SDA / GPIO3 SCL) and logs the values to the console every 500 ms, while checking each driver library or I2C call for errors, detecting a sensor‑absent condition by a NACK on the initial write, handling any bus errors gracefully without crashing, and installing a SIGINT handler so that pressing Ctrl +C cleanly closes the I2C handle and invokes the library’s API call() for proper cleanup.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that opens the I2C bus 1 device file (/dev/i2c-1) with full error checking, sets the Melexis MLX75030 Time‑of‑Flight sensor as the I2C slave using ioctl I2C_SLAVE and verifies that the device responds, then enters a loop that every 500 ms (using nanosleep) reads the distance measurement from the sensor and prints a line to stdout in the form “Distance: <value> mm”; if an I2C read fails the program must write a diagnostic message to stderr and simply continue to the next cycle without exiting, while if the sensor is not present at startup it must print an error and exit with status 1; a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler must be installed so that pressing Ctrl‑C cleanly closes the I2C file descriptor and terminates the program with status 0.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces with a Silicon Labs Si1175 ambient light and proximity sensor over I2C using the documented default address, samples the ambient light value every 5 seconds, and appends each reading to a file named proximity_log.csv with a header row “timestamp,als_visible” where the timestamp is formatted in ISO‑8601; the implementation must check the result of every I2C open, read, and write call, handle the cases where the sensor is absent or the bus reports an error, and ensure that on all exit paths—including receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM—the I2C file descriptor and the log file are cleanly closed, while using only standard POSIX/Linux APIs and including <stdint.h> for the uint8_t/uint16_t types.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads ambient light and proximity data from a Silicon Labs Si1120 sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, sampling every 500 ms and retrying any I2C operation up to three times with a 10 ms delay between attempts, resetting the sensor via register the documented value with command the documented value then verifying that the part ID at register the documented value equals the documented value, combining the ALS and proximity byte pairs into 16‑bit little‑endian values, and appending each reading with a timestamp in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS” to a file named si1120_log.txt; the program must check the result of every initialization and system call, print descriptive error messages to stderr, and on any failure or on normal termination release all resources (the I2C handle, the log file, and the driver library), and it should run until a SIGINT (Ctrl‑C) is received.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that interfaces with a Silicon Labs Si1182‑A‑GM optical sensor over I2C using the /dev/i2c‑1 device, verifies the sensor by reading its part ID register and configuring the measurement rate register to the documented values, then continuously reads ambient light (lux) and proximity data every 100 ms, logging each timestamped reading (formatted as YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS.mmm) to a CSV line in a file named biometric_log.txt as “timestamp,lux,proximity” while also printing the same line to stdout; the program must check every I2C read and write for errors, handle sensor absence when the part ID read fails, report I2C bus errors such as NACK with appropriate messages, and include SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers that close the I2C file descriptor and the log file so that all resources are released on normal and error exits, with proximity recorded as the raw 16‑bit value and all I2C communication performed via standard Linux ioctl calls (open, ioctl, read, write).

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously reads proximity data from a Silicon Labs Si1145 sensor over I2C using the documented address, combines the PS1_DATA0 and PS1_DATA1 registers into a single 16‑bit unsigned proximity value, and appends each reading to a file named proximity_log.txt with a timestamp in the format YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS; the program must check every I2C write and read operation for errors, and on any I2C communication failure it must log the error with a timestamp, retry the operation up to three times and, if the retries are exhausted, exit gracefully, while sensor initialisation failures must be handled with clear error messages; the implementation should rely exclusively on the provided driver API functions for all sensor interactions, avoid any other libraries, and include SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers that on receipt close the I2C handle, close the log file, terminate the driver, and ensure a clean shutdown, allowing the program to run indefinitely until interrupted by Ctrl‑C or a termination signal.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that interfaces with a Sensirion SHT40 humidity and temperature sensor over I2C bus 1 using the SDA pin on GPIO2 (BCM) and the SCL pin on GPIO3 (BCM) at the documented 7‑bit address, issuing the high‑repeatability measurement command (documented value) and then waiting at least 10 ms before reading the 6‑byte result (two bytes temperature MSB+LSB, one CRC, two bytes humidity MSB+LSB, one CRC), validating each reading with the Sensirion CRC‑8 algorithm using the documented polynomial and initial value, and logging timestamped temperature and humidity values to a file named ‘sht40_log.txt’ every 5 seconds; the program must robustly handle errors from opening the I2C device, ioctl calls, writes, and reads by logging an error and retrying on the next cycle, and it must cleanly close both the I2C file descriptor and the log file when receiving SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that periodically reads differential pressure and temperature from a Sensirion SDP31 (±500 Pa) differential pressure sensor on I²C bus 1 using the documented I²C address, triggers continuous measurement with the documented command, waits at least 1 ms after the trigger, then reads the six‑byte response (pressure MSB, pressure LSB, CRC, temperature MSB, temperature LSB, CRC), converts the values to pressure in pascals and temperature in degrees Celsius, and appends a line containing a timestamp, pressure_pa and temperature_c as comma‑separated fields to a file named airflow.log, flushing the file after each write; the sampling interval must be 100 ms, and any I²C write or read failure must be retried up to three times with exponential backoff, using the driver library functions for all sensor interactions, while handling SIGINT and SIGTERM via a volatile sig_atomic_t flag so the main loop can exit cleanly, and on every exit path the program must close the I²C handle, close the log file, and invoke the library’s cleanup API call().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads temperature and humidity from a Silicon Labs Si7015 sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented I2C address, operates the sensor in No Hold Master mode by writing the documented command for temperature or humidity and then polling‑reading the two‑byte result until the measurement is ready (taking no more than about 20 ms per measurement), samples the data every 5 seconds, and logs each reading together with a timestamp to a file named sensor_data.txt opened in append mode while also printing the timestamped values to the console; the program must verify successful initialization of the driver library, opening of the I2C bus, each I2C write and read operation, and opening of the log file, retry transient I2C failures, and terminate cleanly with an error message if the sensor is absent or a bus error occurs, and it must handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) by closing the I2C handle, terminating the driver library, and closing any open file before exiting, using <errno.h> for strerror() as needed.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads differential pressure from the Sensirion SDP800-500Pa sensor over the I2C bus /dev/i2c-1, using the documented I2C address, by first issuing the documented continuous‑measurement trigger command, waiting approximately 45 ms, then reading nine bytes (three‑byte pressure value with CRC, three‑byte temperature value with CRC, and three‑byte scale‑factor value with CRC), validating each CRC‑8 word, and logging every 100 ms a line containing a timestamp, the pressure in pascals, and the temperature in degrees Celsius as comma‑separated values to a file named “airflow_data.txt” that begins with a header row; the program must check the result of every system call, handle sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions gracefully, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM cleanly release all resources, and it should include the appropriate Linux I2C header (e.g., <linux/the driver library.h>) while using only the Linux I2C syscalls for communication.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that periodically samples temperature from a Sensirion STS30‑DIS temperature‑only sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented default address, issuing the single‑shot high‑repeatability measurement command (documented value), then waiting at least 15 ms for conversion before reading the three‑byte response (two data bytes and one CRC byte) and validating the CRC‑8 checksum with the documented polynomial and initial value; the program must record each successful reading with an ISO‑8601 timestamp to a file named enclosure_temp_log.txt, implement robust error handling for any I2C communication failures—including initialization, write, read, or CRC mismatch—logging each error with a timestamp to error_log.txt, and must handle SIGINT to perform a graceful shutdown that closes all file handles and releases any resources cleanly on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that interfaces with a Sensirion SCD40 CO₂ sensor over I²C bus 1 using the documented 100 kHz clock‑stretching‑compatible speed and the sensor’s documented address, starts periodic measurement, waits at least one second before the first read, then every five seconds polls the documented data‑ready flag and, only when the flag indicates data is ready, reads the documented 9‑byte block (six data bytes plus three CRC bytes), verifies each 2‑byte word with the documented CRC‑8 polynomial and initialization values, extracts the raw CO₂ value in ppm, temperature in °C and humidity in % directly from the data, and appends a line to “air_quality.log” in CSV format containing a timestamp, CO₂_ppm, Temperature_C and Humidity_pct with an immediate flush; the program must check every return value from the driver initialization, I²C opening, command transmission and CRC checks, printing a descriptive error to stderr and either retrying or exiting as appropriate, and on receipt of SIGINT it must send the documented Stop Periodic Measurement command, close the I²C handle, terminate the driver, close the log file and exit cleanly, all while ensuring the sensor has ambient light for its photoacoustic measurement to function correctly in the smart ventilation air‑quality monitor.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that communicates with a Sensirion SCD40 CO2 sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, reads CO2, temperature and humidity every 5 seconds, validates the CRC‑8 checksum on each 2‑byte data word, and stores each reading in a circular buffer in RAM sized for 20 entries while also printing every valid reading to stdout; the program must verify that the I2C driver and sensor initialization succeed, check the return value of every I2C write and read operation, and gracefully handle cases where the sensor is absent or the bus reports errors without crashing, and it must drive a CO2 warning LED connected to GPIO17 (BCM numbering) turning the LED on whenever the CO2 concentration exceeds 1000 ppm and off otherwise, and finally it must install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that on termination stops the sensor, closes the I2C handle, releases the GPIO, and shuts down the driver cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads temperature from an Analog Devices TMP05 digital temperature sensor by polling its PWM‑style output on GPIO4 (BCM, physical pin 7), measuring the high‑pulse width and total cycle width with a busy‑wait loop using microsecond‑resolution timestamps obtained from the library’s call() API, sampling once every 5 seconds and applying a 50 ms timeout on each edge wait; the program must verify that the driver library initializes correctly and that the log file “temperature_log.txt” opens in append mode, compute the temperature while guarding against division by zero if the low‑time (TL) is zero, flag any reading outside the valid range of –40 °C to +150 °C as an error, and after three consecutive failures write a “SENSOR MALFUNCTION” entry to the log, logging each valid reading together with an ISO‑8601 timestamp; it must also handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a clean shutdown by closing the file and releasing the driver library resources.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads temperature and humidity from a Sensirion SHT35‑DIS‑B sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented high‑repeatability, clock‑stretching‑disabled measurement command, validates the 8‑bit CRC for both the temperature and humidity words, and, after waiting at least 15 ms for the 6‑byte result, converts the raw values to degrees Celsius and percent relative humidity with the standard Sensirion formulas, then adds a sinusoidal offset of ±2 °C and ±5 % RH over a one‑hour period to simulate a greenhouse environment before logging each reading with an ISO‑8601 UTC timestamp to a file named “environmental_data.txt” every 5 seconds; if any I2C read/write or CRC check fails, the program must retry up to three times with a one‑second delay and, after exhausting retries, log NaN values, while also providing robust error handling for driver initialization, I2C open/read/write, and file open, and must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to gracefully shut down by closing the I2C handle, flushing and closing the log file, and terminating the driver cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that interfaces with the Sensirion SDP810-125Pa differential pressure sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented I2C address, sends the documented continuous measurement command, waits the approximately 45 ms conversion time, then reads the 9‑byte block containing pressure, temperature and scale factor each followed by an 8‑bit CRC‑8 checksum (using the polynomial and initial value documented for the sensor), validates those CRCs, converts the raw data to pressure in pascals and temperature in degrees Celsius with the sensor‑specified formulas, and logs a timestamp together with the pressure and temperature values to a CSV file named “airflow.csv” at a rate of one entry per second; the program must also detect and handle sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM perform a graceful shutdown that closes the I2C file descriptor and any open file handles.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously reads temperature and humidity from a Sensirion SHT35‑DIS‑B sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented single‑shot high‑repeatability measurement command with clock‑stretching disabled, waiting at least 15 ms after issuing the command before reading the six‑byte result, sampling every five seconds, validating both CRC‑8 checksums with the documented polynomial and initial value, and logging each reading to a CSV file named environment.csv with an ISO‑8601 timestamp followed by temperature in Celsius and relative humidity in percent, inserting a header row if the file does not already exist or is empty; the program must check the driver initialization, opening of the I2C bus, every I2C read/write operation, CRC validation, and file opening, printing a descriptive error to stderr on any failure and either continuing or exiting as appropriate, and it must install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that performs a clean shutdown by closing the I2C handle and invoking the sensor library’s shutdown call.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that periodically reads temperature and humidity from an Adafruit Si7021 temperature and humidity sensor on I2C bus 1 (GPIO 2/3) using the documented I2C address, polling each measurement until data is available or a 100 ms timeout expires, reading three bytes (MSB, LSB, CRC) for each value and verifying the CRC‑8 checksum with the documented polynomial and initial value, logging a line every 5 seconds to a CSV file named environment.log with a header “timestamp,temperature_C,humidity_percent” and ISO‑8601 timestamps, writing “ERROR” in place of the numeric fields together with a descriptive message to stderr whenever an I2C or CRC error occurs, checking the return value of every system call, handling sensor‑absent conditions such as I2C open failure or NACK, and on any read failure issuing the documented sensor reset command before the next cycle; the program must also install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that cleanly closes the I2C file descriptor and exits gracefully, thereby simulating a greenhouse monitoring system.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads differential pressure and temperature from a Sensirion SDP810-500Pa sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented I2C address, initiates continuous measurement with the documented command, waits the required conversion time, then reads the 9‑byte response containing pressure MSB, pressure LSB, CRC, temperature MSB, temperature LSB, CRC and three scale‑factor bytes, validates the CRC‑8 for both pressure and temperature raw values, converts the raw data to floating‑point pressure (Pa) and temperature (°C), and logs each sample once per second to a binary file named airflow.dat with pressure followed by temperature as floats while keeping the file handle open across samples; the program must check driver initialization, I2C opening, command write and read results, handle sensor‑absent and bus‑error conditions, and implement signal handling for SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that closes the I2C handle, terminates the driver, and closes the file on all exit paths.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads CO₂, temperature and humidity from a Sensirion SCD30 CO₂ sensor on the I2C bus, samples the data every 5 seconds, and writes each sample to an air_quality.log file as a CSV line containing an ISO 8601 UTC timestamp followed by CO₂ in ppm, temperature in °C and humidity in %RH, flushing the log after each write; the program must implement ventilation control logic where CO₂ below 800 ppm results in an OFF state, between 800 ppm and 1199 ppm a LOW state, and 1200 ppm or above a HIGH state, and must robustly handle driver library initialization failures, I2C open/write/read errors, sensor non‑response, data‑not‑ready conditions and CRC mismatches by logging the error and continuing without crashing; a sigaction handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM must stop the periodic measurement, close the I2C handle, close the log file and invoke the library’s cleanup API call before exiting, and when the program is run in a mocked or emulated environment with no hardware it should log the lack of sensor access and exit gracefully with return code 0 rather than aborting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that periodically reads the differential pressure from a Sensirion SDP32 (±125 Pa) sensor over the I2C bus, using a default sampling interval of 1000 ms that can be overridden with a command‑line argument, and prints each reading to the console with a timestamp; each reading must consist of exactly nine bytes – pressure MSB, pressure LSB, pressure CRC‑8, temperature MSB, temperature LSB, temperature CRC‑8, scale‑factor MSB, scale‑factor LSB, scale‑factor CRC‑8 – and the program must verify the CRC‑8 for the pressure, temperature, and scale‑factor words, handle I2C failures robustly by detecting sensor‑absent and bus‑error conditions, emit a clear diagnostic message and exit if the sensor is not connected, and ensure that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path by installing appropriate signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM so that the program terminates with exit code 0 on those signals while still exiting with an error code on unrecoverable I2C errors.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that periodically reads the differential pressure and temperature from a Sensirion SDP810-125Pa differential pressure sensor on the I2C bus (bus 1) using SDA on GPIO2 (BCM) and SCL on GPIO3 (BCM), waiting at least 45 ms after each trigger for the conversion to complete and then logging the results to stdout once every second; the implementation must open the I2C bus, verify successful driver initialization, perform a 9‑byte read that contains pressure, temperature and their respective scale factors, validate the CRC‑8 on each 3‑byte word using the documented polynomial and initial value, handle any CRC mismatch, sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions on every read/write, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM close the I2C handle and invoke the library’s cleanup API on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B running a 64‑bit kernel that periodically reads temperature and humidity from a Texas Instruments HDC1000 sensor attached via I2C on bus 1, with SDA on GPIO2 (BCM) and SCL on GPIO3 (BCM); the program must wait at least 20 ms after initiating a 14‑bit temperature and humidity conversion before reading the result, then log the values to the console every 5 seconds in the format “Temperature: XX.XX C, Humidity: XX.XX %”, while checking the return value of every open(), ioctl(), read() and write() call, handling the case where the sensor is absent (device file cannot be opened or no ACK is received) and, on any read failure, printing an error message to stderr and continuing the loop, and finally installing handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that close the I2C file descriptor before exiting, noting that the DRDYn pin is not connected and the fixed delay must be relied upon for conversion timing.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously reads temperature and humidity from a Texas Instruments HDC2010 sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, polling the sensor’s MEASUREMENT_CONFIG register until bit 0 clears or a timeout of roughly 500 ms occurs, then outputs the readings to the console every five seconds; the implementation must check the result of every driver call, detect a missing sensor (NAK) and any bus‑error conditions, retry transient I2C failures only up to a defined maximum count, and include a clean shutdown triggered by Ctrl +C via a signal handler that sets a volatile sig_atomic_t flag, closes the I2C handle, and invokes the library’s API call() before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that periodically reads the differential pressure from a Sensirion SDP800-500Pa on I2C bus 1 using the documented I2C address, waits approximately 45 ms for each measurement to complete, and logs to the console the raw 16‑bit pressure and temperature values every 500 ms; the program must open the I2C bus, verify that the driver library initializes correctly, check the result of every write and read operation, read exactly six bytes (two bytes pressure, one CRC, two bytes temperature, one CRC), validate each CRC‑8 checksum using the documented polynomial and initial value, handle sensor‑absent and bus‑error conditions gracefully, and on receipt of a SIGINT perform a clean shutdown by closing the I2C handle and invoking the library’s cleanup API on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that implements a PID‑controlled reflow oven using a MAX6675 thermocouple amplifier and a solid‑state relay, communicating with the MAX6675 over SPI0 (using either CE0 or CE1 as appropriate) and driving the solid‑state relay from GPIO17 (BCM numbering); the program must read the temperature from the thermocouple at a 1 Hz rate, update the SSR duty cycle based on the PID output (scaled 0.0 to 1.0) over a 1‑second period, log each temperature reading to a file named reflow_log.csv, load the target temperature profile from profile.txt where each line contains time_seconds,target_temp_celsius, apply robust error handling for all SPI communication and GPIO control including sensor‑absent and bus‑error conditions, and ensure that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path by handling termination signals.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that implements a PID‑controlled greenhouse heater using a DS18B20 temperature sensor and a 12 V heater driven through a relay and hardware PWM; the DS18B20 data line must be connected to GPIO4 (physical pin 7) on the 1‑wire bus accessed via the w1‑gpio kernel module at /sys/bus/w1/devices/, the relay enable line to GPIO17 (physical pin 11), and the PWM duty control to GPIO18 (physical pin 12) using the hardware PWM channel, while the program must accept command‑line arguments specifying the desired temperature setpoint and the PID gains Kp, Ki, and Kd, read the sensor periodically, validate the CRC of each DS18B20 reading and handle sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions, compute the PID output, set the appropriate PWM duty cycle and relay state, and log every 5 seconds to a file named greenhouse.log a line containing the timestamp, average temperature, setpoint, PID output and PWM duty cycle; all I/O operations must be checked for errors, and the program must install SIGINT/SIGTERM handlers that on any exit path cleanly release resources by turning off the relay, setting PWM to zero, closing any opened file descriptors or device handles, and closing the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that continuously reads humidity from an AHT20 sensor on the I2C bus /dev/i2c-1 using the documented address, triggering a measurement, waiting 80 ms, then reading the 6‑byte result while verifying that the status byte reports calibrated and not busy, retrying any failed I2C transaction up to three times with a 10 ms pause between attempts, and logging each humidity reading together with a timestamp to the console; the program must poll the sensor every 5 seconds, activate a dehumidifier relay connected to GPIO17 (active‑high) whenever the humidity exceeds 60 % and deactivate it when the humidity falls below 55 %, handle the case where the sensor is absent or all retries fail by printing an error message to stderr without terminating, and respond to SIGINT and SIGTERM by cleanly releasing the GPIO line, closing the I2C file descriptor and exiting with status 0.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously reads the CPU temperature from the thermal zone file /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp, maps the temperature linearly to a PWM duty cycle on GPIO18 (BCM) with a 25 kHz frequency and a 0‑255 range such that 40 °C corresponds to 0 % duty, 70 °C to 100 % duty and values are clamped below 40 °C and above 70 °C, drives a PWM‑controlled cooling fan accordingly, logs every 5 seconds to a file named fan_log.txt the current timestamp, temperature and duty cycle, and includes robust error handling for failures to read the temperature, write to the log file, or initialize the PWM driver, while also installing signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that gracefully stop the fan, close any open files and terminate the PWM driver before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads temperature and pressure from a Bosch BMP280 sensor connected on I2C bus 1 (/dev/i2c-1, SDA on GPIO2 pin 3, SCL on GPIO3 pin 5) using the documented default address when SDO is tied to GND and falling back to the documented alternative address, applies the Bosch 64‑bit compensation formulas, rewrites the ctrl_meas register in forced mode each loop to trigger a new measurement, and appends a line to weather_data.txt every five seconds in the exact format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS, Temperature: XX.XX °C, Pressure: YYYY.YY hPa”, while checking every I/O call (open, ioctl, read, write, fopen, fputs) for errors, logging any sensor I/O failures to stderr and attempting to continue or exit gracefully, ensuring the sensor is powered from the 3.3 V rail only, and handling SIGINT and SIGTERM to break the logging loop, close the I2C file descriptor and any open files, and exit with status 0.

prompt: Write a C program for the Raspberry Pi 5 that actively manages the official Raspberry Pi 5 Active Cooler by reading the CPU temperature from /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp and the current fan state from /sys/class/thermal/cooling_device0/cur_state, polling the temperature every 5 seconds, applying a tiered speed map where temperatures below 45 °C set the fan state to 0 (off), below 55 °C set state 1, below 65 °C set state 2, and 65 °C or higher set state 3 (maximum), first validating the cooling device’s max_state before any write, and writing the new state back to the same cooling_device sysfs entry only when the speed changes; each fan speed change must be logged with a timestamp to /var/log/fan_control.log, all file opens, reads, writes, and parses must be checked for errors with transient read failures simply causing the program to retry on the next cycle, and the program must handle graceful shutdown on SIGINT or SIGTERM by setting the fan to state 0, logging the shutdown event, and exiting cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that implements a PID controller to maintain a target temperature of 50 °C by PWM‑controlling a resistive heater on GPIO18 using hardware PWM at 1 kHz with a duty range of 0‑100 %; the program must read the current temperature from a MAX31855 thermocouple amplifier connected on SPI0 (CLK = GPIO11, CS = GPIO8/CE0, DO = GPIO9) at 500 kHz, acquiring 4 bytes per sample, and log every second to a file named heater_log.txt the measured temperature, the PWM duty cycle, and the PID output; the PID defaults are Kp = 1.0, Ki = 0.1, Kd = 0.01, and the controller must include error handling that parses the MAX31855 fault bits to detect open‑circuit, short‑to‑GND, or short‑to‑VCC conditions, logs any such errors, disables the heater and resets the PID state, and also enforces a failsafe that disables the heater if the reading exceeds 100 °C or falls below 0 °C; finally, the program must cleanly release resources on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM by turning the heater off, closing the SPI interface, and terminating any driver activity.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the GPIO bus to drive the PWM input of a Noctua NF‑A4x10 5V PWM fan connected to GPIO18 (physical pin 12), polling the CPU temperature every 5 seconds and mapping the temperature linearly to a 25 kHz PWM duty cycle where temperatures of 40 °C and below correspond to 0 % duty, 70 °C and above correspond to 100 % duty, and values in between are interpolated accordingly; the program must verify that the driver library initializes correctly, confirm that each PWM frequency and duty cycle call succeeds, and log each reading to a file named cooling_log.csv with a header and rows containing the timestamp, temperature in °C, and the PWM duty cycle percentage, while also handling any file I/O errors, and it must clean up gracefully on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM by turning the fan off and releasing all resources.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that runs as a daemon and continuously polls the SEN0193 Water Level Sensor (digital output) connected to the GPIO bus on pin GPIO23 (BCM numbering), using a pull‑down resistor on the input to keep the line low when dry, reading the sensor every 2 seconds and generating an alert whenever a logic HIGH is detected; on each detection the program must print an alert message to stdout and append a line to a file named flood_log.txt in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS ALERT: Water detected”, while also checking that the driver library initializes correctly and, if a GPIO read fails, logging an error entry to the same file and scheduling an automatic re‑initialization attempt after 60 seconds; the daemon must also handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to release all resources cleanly before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B running Bookworm or later that reads the RPM from a Melexis MLX90217 Hall‑effect sensor connected to the GPIO bus, with the sensor output wired to physical pin 7 (BCM GPIO4), by configuring the pin as an input with the internal pull‑up resistor enabled and counting rising‑edge pulses using GPIO interrupts; the program must count pulses in a one‑second window using an atomic add for the pulse counter, compute the revolutions per minute, and log one sample per second to a file named rpm_log.txt in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS <rpm>” while also printing the same line to stdout, flushing the file after each write; it must check every driver‑library call and the file‑open call for errors, exiting with a diagnostic message on failure, but if the sensor is absent or not rotating it should log an RPM of 0 instead of aborting; finally, the program must install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers that disable the timer and alert callback, close the log file, and invoke the library’s cleanup API call before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that monitors a rotating shaft’s RPM by reading two DRV5032FJDBZR Hall‑Effect sensors connected to the GPIO bus, with sensor 1 wired to GPIO17 (BCM) and sensor 2 to GPIO18 (BCM), applying approximately a 5 ms debounce to each state change, logging every transition to a CSV file named shaft_log.txt in the format “timestamp,sensor1_state,sensor2_state”, printing the calculated RPM to the console, handling any GPIO initialization failures or file I/O errors gracefully, including the standard headers such as errno.h and string.h to ensure clean compilation, and guaranteeing that all resources are released properly on every exit path, including handling SIGINT (Ctrl+C) to perform orderly cleanup.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads heart rate and SpO2 data from a Silicon Labs Si1182 I2C optical sensor on I2C bus 1, pausing one second between each read, and appends each measurement to a file named biometric_log.txt in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS, Heart Rate: X BPM, SpO2: Y%%” while flushing the file after every write; the program must use the driver library for I2C access, check the return value of every I2C read and write operation, print any communication errors to stderr and keep running, and it must also install a SIGINT handler so that when Ctrl‑C is pressed it gracefully shuts down by closing the I2C handle, closing the log file, and terminating the driver library before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously monitors three Texas Instruments TMAG5110A1 Hall‑Effect latch sensors connected on the GPIO bus, with sensor 1 OUT wired to GPIO4 (BCM), sensor 2 OUT to GPIO17 (BCM) and sensor 3 OUT to GPIO27 (BCM), configuring each pin as an input with an internal pull‑up enabled and verifying that every GPIO mode/pull call returns 0; the sensors use an open‑drain output that pulls the line low when a south pole is present (magnet‑present = logic low) and releases it high when the magnet is removed (magnet‑removed = logic high), so the program must poll the pins every 100 ms using the library’s API call, record the initial state on the first read without generating a false transition, and thereafter log each state change with an ISO‑8601 timestamp and the corresponding sensor identifier to a file named magnet_log.txt, while handling any sensor read errors gracefully by writing an error message to stderr and continuing operation; additionally, install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers that perform a clean shutdown by closing the log file and invoking the library’s API call() before exit, and include comments in the source explaining the latch behavior.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that continuously drives a common‑cathode RGB LED attached to the GPIO bus, with the red channel on GPIO24 (physical pin 18, BCM), green on GPIO23 (physical pin 16, BCM) and blue on GPIO18 (physical pin 12, BCM), using software PWM implemented in a simple timing loop (no hardware PWM) at 100 Hz (10 ms period) for each channel, generating random intensity values from 0 to 100 for each colour using rand() seeded with time(NULL) and changing the colour randomly every 100 ms; the program must check the library's API call() for each line, check the library's API call() for each line, check the library's API call() for each line and report descriptive error messages on failure, employ a busy‑wait PWM loop with clock_nanosleep for sub‑millisecond precision (no sleep calls shorter than 1 ms), run indefinitely until the user presses Ctrl+C, and on receipt of SIGINT invoke a signal handler that cleanly releases all GPIO lines and exits, ensuring proper resource cleanup on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously polls an Adafruit LSM303DLHC accelerometer on I2C bus 1 at 10 Hz, computes the total G‑force magnitude, and when that magnitude exceeds a configurable threshold (default 2.0 G, settable with a ‑t command‑line argument) triggers an impact interrupt by setting GPIO17 (BCM numbering) as an output and pulsing it HIGH for 50 ms, while also logging the timestamped accelerometer data to a file named impact_log.txt; the program must check the result of every I2C read and write operation, handle cases where the sensor is absent or the bus reports errors, and ensure that on any exit path—including receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM—it cleanly releases all resources such as the I2C handle, the GPIO pin, and any driver state.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads ambient light and color data from an Analog Devices ADPD188BI optical sensor on I2C bus 1, samples the sensor every 500 ms, combines the ALS LSB and MSB into a 16‑bit unsigned value, and logs each timestamped reading of ALS, red, green and blue channels to a CSV file named color_log.csv with a header row; the program must also control an LED connected to GPIO18 (BCM) using hardware PWM so that brighter ambient light increases the LED brightness, handle any I2C errors such as failed writes, reads or a missing sensor by writing an error message to stderr and retrying after a 100 ms delay, and implement signal handling for SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that closes the I2C handle, turns off the LED and closes the CSV file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously reads the Adafruit FXOS8700CQ 6‑Axis Accelerometer/Magnetometer over I2C bus 1 at a 50 ms interval, first verifying the WHO_AM_I identifier on startup and aborting with a clear error message if it does not match, then placing the device in standby, configuring the sensor for a ±2 g range, and finally activating it for a 200 Hz output data rate; each loop must compute the acceleration magnitude from the three axes, and whenever the magnitude exceeds a defined impact threshold the program should append a line to “impact_log.txt” containing the current timestamp and the raw x, y, z values and the computed magnitude formatted as “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS,x,y,z,magnitude” with three decimal places, while checking the return value of every I2C call, printing a diagnostic to stderr on read errors and continuing the loop rather than crashing, and the application must handle SIGINT (Ctrl‑C) by gracefully closing the I2C handle, invoking the appropriate library shutdown call, and exiting cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that interfaces over I2C bus 1 with a GY-50 L3G4200D gyroscope, performs a 100‑sample stationary calibration at startup to compute X, Y and Z zero‑rate offsets, then continuously reads angular velocity, applies the offsets, and logs the calibrated X, Y, Z values together with ISO‑8601 timestamps to a file named gyro_log.txt at a 20 Hz rate (50 ms period), appending an alert line to the same log whenever any axis exceeds 50 dps and also printing a warning to stderr for the same condition; the program must verify the result of every open, ioctl, read and write call, detect sensor absence by reading the WHO_AM_I register and confirming the documented value, handle any I2C bus errors, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM cleanly close the I2C file descriptor and the log file before exiting.
pinned_library: Linux i2c-dev ioctl interface (/dev/i2c-1 character device)

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads acceleration data from an ADXL345 accelerometer on I2C bus 1 every 100 ms (10 Hz), verifies that the device ID register returns the documented value before any sampling, and logs each sample to a file named accel_log.txt in the format “timestamp,x,y,z” with the three axis values expressed in g units to three decimal places; the program must configure the ADXL345 for full‑resolution mode with a ±2 g range, check the result of every I2C call and avoid writing any garbage to the log on read failures, turn on an active‑high LED connected to GPIO17 (BCM numbering) whenever the absolute acceleration on any axis exceeds 2.0 g and turn it off otherwise, and cleanly release the I2C handle, GPIO, and close the log file when receiving SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads data from a GY-51 LSM303DLHC accelerometer and magnetometer connected on I2C bus 1, samples the sensors every 100 ms, computes a tilt‑compensated heading, and logs each sample with a timestamp, the heading, the three‑axis acceleration in g, and the three‑axis magnetic field in gauss to a file named compass_log.txt, adding a CSV header when the file is created; the program must check the result of every I2C operation and handle cases where the sensor is absent or the bus reports an error, and it must install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that closes the I2C handles and terminates the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously reads distance from an Adafruit VL6180X Time‑of‑Flight sensor on I2C bus 1, performing the sensor’s mandatory initialization sequence before use, sampling the range every 100 ms, and writing each timestamped reading to a file named distance_log.txt while also logging the string “DOOR_OPEN” whenever the measured distance is less than 100 mm and “DOOR_CLOSED” otherwise; the code must check every I2C read and write return value, detect sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions and attempt to re‑initialize the sensor in those cases, and must install a SIGINT handler that cleanly releases all resources before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that samples two STMicroelectronics IMP23ABSU Ultrasonic MEMS Microphone sensors connected on I2C bus 1 at a 10 ms sampling interval, reads 16‑bit signed audio samples from each sensor, timestamps each pair of samples using CLOCK_REALTIME, computes the time‑difference‑of‑arrival (TDOA) between the two channels, and appends a line to a CSV‑formatted file named audio_log.dat with the columns sec,nsec,sensor1,sensor2,tdoa; the implementation must verify that all driver library initialization and I2C communication calls succeed, and if a sensor is absent or the bus fails it must gracefully skip that sample and retry, while a SIGINT signal handler must guarantee clean release of I2C handles, closure of the log file, and termination of the driver library on any exit path.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that periodically reads the gyroscope and accelerometer data from an Analog Devices ADIS16448 IMU over SPI channel 0 using CE0 on GPIO8 (BCM), operating at 1 MHz in SPI Mode 0, and prints the six values (gyro x, y, z and accel x, y, z) to the console every 100 ms; the read sequence must follow the two‑cycle protocol where the first 16‑bit transfer sends the read command (register address with bit 15 set), then after a stall time of at least 40 µs a second 16‑bit transfer sends the documented dummy value to clock out the 16‑bit data, which should be scaled using 0.05 deg/sec per LSB for the gyroscope and 0.00025 g per LSB for the accelerometer, and the implementation must include robust error handling for driver library initialization, SPI opening, and any transfer failures, while also handling a Ctrl‑C interrupt cleanly by closing the SPI handle and invoking the library’s API call() before exit.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads the raw 16‑bit signed accelerometer and gyroscope values from a TDK MPU‑6886 6‑axis IMU over I2C bus 1 every 50 ms and prints those values to the console, checking every I2C system call for errors, retrying any transient read failure up to three times, and handling sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions gracefully, while also ensuring that the I2C file descriptor is cleanly closed on all exit paths, including when the program receives a SIGINT (Ctrl‑C).

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously polls an Adafruit ADXL345 accelerometer on I2C bus 1 every 10 ms in full‑resolution mode with a ±2 g range (scale factor 256 LSB/g), verifies that the device ID register returns the documented value and checks the result of every I2C read or write, and when the computed total acceleration magnitude exceeds a 2.5 g threshold it turns on a red LED connected to GPIO17 (BCM) for 500 ms, records the event to a file named impact_log.txt with a timestamp and the magnitude together with the X, Y and Z components, and ensures that on normal exit or on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM all resources—including the I2C handle, the LED GPIO, the log file and any driver state—are cleanly released, while also handling sensor‑absent and bus‑error conditions according to the verification steps.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that opens I2C bus 1 to communicate with a TDK InvenSense ICM‑20602 IMU, performs burst reads of the six accelerometer bytes and six gyroscope bytes at a 10 Hz rate (every 100 ms), checks the return value of every I2C operation and prints any failures to stderr, timestamps each sample and appends the x, y, z accelerometer and gyroscope values to a file named imu_log.csv, and handles Ctrl +C (SIGINT) gracefully by closing the I2C handle, terminating the driver library, and closing the CSV file before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously reads acceleration data from a GY-45 MMA8451Q accelerometer on I2C bus 1, verifies the sensor’s identity by reading its identification register and confirming the documented value before proceeding, polls the sensor every 100 ms, and whenever the magnitude on any axis exceeds the 2.0 g threshold (with the default ±2 g range where 1 g equals 1024 counts) it turns on an LED connected to GPIO17 (BCM numbering) for 500 ms while logging each reading with a timestamp to a file named impact_log.txt; the program must handle I2C read/write errors gracefully and, on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM, cleanly release the I2C bus, GPIO lines and close the log file.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the GPIO bus to alternately actuate two 12 V DC push‑pull solenoids driven through TIP120 transistors with flyback diodes, assigning solenoid 1 to GPIO17 (BCM) and solenoid 2 to GPIO27 (BCM); the program must set both lines LOW before entering the main loop so that no solenoid is energized at startup, then repeatedly switch the active line with a 500 ms delay implemented via nanosleep, checking every driver library call for errors and printing a diagnostic to stderr on failure, and it must install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that, on Ctrl +C, cleanly releases both lines by setting them LOW and frees all driver library resources before exiting.
raw:
```
$ gcc -Wall -Wextra -Werror -std=c11 -o solenoids solenoids.c -lpigpio -lrt
$ ./solenoids
```

### Solution:
```
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <signal.h>
#include <pigpio.h>

#define SOL1 17
#define SOL2 27

void solenoid_handler(int sig)
{
	gpioWrite(SOL1, 0);
	gpioWrite(SOL2, 0);
	gpioTerminate();
	exit(EXIT_SUCCESS);
}

int main(void)
{
	if (gpioInitialise() < 0) {
		fprintf(stderr, "gpioInitialise() failed\n");
		exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
	}

	gpioSetMode(SOL1, PI_OUTPUT);
	gpioSetMode(SOL2, PI_OUTPUT);

	gpioWrite(SOL1, 0);
	gpioWrite(SOL2, 0);

	signal(SIGINT, solenoid_handler);
	signal(SIGTERM, solenoid_handler);

	while (1) {
		gpioWrite(SOL1, 1);
		gpioWrite(SOL2, 0);
		nanosleep((const struct timespec[]){{0, 500000000L}}, NULL);
		gpioWrite(SOL1, 0);
		gpioWrite(SOL2, 1);
		nanosleep((const struct timespec[]){{0, 500000000L}}, NULL);
	}

	return EXIT_SUCCESS;
}
```

### Explanation:
The program uses the pigpio library to set up the GPIO lines and install a signal handler to cleanly release the GPIO lines and terminate the program. The program then enters a loop that alternately switches the active line with a 500 ms delay implemented via nanosleep.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads angular velocity data from an MPU‑6050 gyroscope over the I2C bus using the hardware I2C1 lines (SDA on GPIO2 (BCM) and SCL on GPIO3 (BCM)), stores the samples in a 100‑sample in‑memory circular buffer, and invokes a user‑defined callback whenever the absolute angular velocity (the magnitude of the X, Y, Z vector) exceeds 50.0 degrees/second; the implementation must open the I2C device with open(), select the MPU‑6050 with ioctl(I2C_SLAVE), perform reads and writes with read() and write(), close the descriptor with close(), include robust error handling for any I2C communication failures such as a missing sensor, bus errors, or read/write failures, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including a graceful shutdown when a SIGINT (Ctrl+C) is received.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads CO₂ concentration from an MH‑Z19B sensor over UART using the device /dev/serial0 configured at 9600 baud with TXD on GPIO14 (BCM) and RXD on GPIO15 (BCM), waits roughly 100 ms for the sensor response, retries partial reads until the full 9‑byte response is obtained or a 1‑second timeout expires, and samples every 5 seconds; each reading must be written as a single‑line JSON object containing a microsecond‑resolution timestamp, the ppm value, and an error flag to a file named co2_log.json (flushed after each write) and also printed to stdout to simulate a remote API call, while any checksum mismatches or other failures are logged with timestamps to co2_error.log; the program must check the return values of all driver calls, the API calls, and file operations, skip a reading on checksum error, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM cleanly close the UART and both log files and terminate the driver library; it must send exactly the documented 9‑byte command sequence, read exactly 9 bytes per response, use only the provided driver API calls (no other userspace driver access), avoid manual GPIO configuration for TXD/RXD, and be compiled with gcc ‑Wall ‑Wextra ‑o co2_monitor co2_monitor.c ‑lthe driver library ‑lrt.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that continuously reads the ambient light level from a BH1750 ambient light sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, waits at least 120 ms after initiating each conversion, and every second logs to a file named lighting_log.txt the current timestamp, the measured lux value, and the states of three 5 V relay‑controlled RGB lamp channels whose relays are wired to GPIO 17 (RED), GPIO 27 (GREEN) and GPIO 22 (BLUE) using BCM numbering; the program must turn on the RED relay when lux is below 50, the GREEN relay when lux is between 50 and 150, the BLUE relay when lux is between 150 and 300, and activate all three relays when lux exceeds 300, while checking all I2C operations and file I/O for errors, handling cases where the sensor is absent or the bus reports errors, and ensuring that on any exit path—including termination via signals—all resources such as the GPIO lines, the I2C file descriptor and the log file are cleanly released.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that implements a smart home lighting system with a sunrise/sunset fade driven by a 24‑hour schedule file named lighting_schedule.txt, where each line follows the format HH:MM:SS,relay_number,on/off; the program must control four relay‑controlled lamp actuators connected to GPIO4, GPIO17, GPIO27, and GPIO22 (BCM numbering), checking the schedule file every second, and when a transition is required it must perform a 1800‑second (30‑minute) fade using 100 Hz PWM to vary lamp brightness with a duty cycle ranging from 0 to 100; it must handle file read errors, GPIO initialization failures, and invalid schedule entries gracefully, and must install signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that cleanly turn off all relays and release GPIO resources on exit while avoiding any non‑reentrant functions such as fopen or localtime inside those handlers.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that implements a rudimentary theremin by reading distance from an HC‑SR04 ultrasonic distance sensor and mapping it to a PWM buzzer frequency, using GPIO23 (BCM) for the trigger output, GPIO24 (BCM) for the echo input, and GPIO18 (BCM) for the PWM buzzer output; the program must issue a 10 µs trigger pulse via the library’s API, obtain microsecond‑precision echo timing through the same API, run a main loop at roughly 50 Hz while enforcing a minimum 60 ms gap between successive measurements, clamp the computed frequency to the buzzer’s valid range before applying it, provide robust error handling for driver initialization and HC‑SR04 readings—including detection of a missing sensor and timeout conditions—with any failures logged to stderr, and clean up gracefully on SIGINT by silencing the buzzer and deinitializing the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that drives a common‑anode RGB LED using hardware PWM at a 1 kHz frequency on the BCM pins where red is on GPIO17, green on GPIO22 and blue on GPIO27, generating a smooth color transition that reflects a simulated proximity value ranging from 0.0 to 1.0 (for example a sine‑wave function over time) rather than any external input, while handling driver library initialization errors gracefully, checking the result of every GPIO operation, and ensuring that on all exit paths—including a SIGINT interrupt—the LED is turned off and the PWM resources are released with the appropriate library call.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads angular velocity from an MPU‑6050 gyroscope over the I2C bus /dev/i2c‑1 using the documented device address, with SDA connected to GPIO2 (BCM) and SCL to GPIO3 (BCM), samples the sensor every 100 ms, and appends to a file named gyro_log.txt a timestamp followed by the x, y, and z axis values in degrees per second; the program must robustly handle all I/O and I2C errors by checking the return values of open, ioctl, read and write calls and must also detect and manage the case where the sensor is absent, and it should cleanly close all file descriptors and terminate gracefully when receiving SIGINT or SIGTERM, while no network logging or configuration file parsing is required.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that monitors a button wired to GPIO17 (BCM) with its internal pull‑up enabled and active‑low, debounces it with at least a 50 ms interval, and on each valid press triggers a musical doorbell by playing a stored melody from a const melody lookup table through a piezo buzzer connected to the hardware PWM0 output on GPIO18 (BCM) using the library's API call() to generate tones at a 50 % duty cycle for volume; the ISR must be non‑blocking and set a volatile flag that the main loop checks to start or, if a second press occurs during playback, gracefully stop the melody, and the program must include proper error handling for every the driver library call (the library's API call, the library's API call, the library's API call, the library's API call), as well as handling SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a clean shutdown by stopping PWM, releasing resources, and calling the library's API call.
