Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads the angular velocity from an MPU‑6050 gyroscope over the hardware I2C bus /dev/i2c‑1 using the documented device address, with SDA connected to GPIO2 (BCM) and SCL to GPIO3 (BCM); the program must continuously acquire the x, y, and z axis rotation rates and log those three values to the console, while checking the result of every I2C read and write system call and handling any sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions gracefully, and it must also install signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM so that all resources are cleanly released on any exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that implements an automated plant watering system by sequentially activating four 5 V relay modules connected to GPIO17, GPIO18, GPIO27 and GPIO22 (BCM numbers, physical pins 11, 12, 13, 15); the program must open the library’s API, request all four lines as outputs with active‑low semantics, set all lines HIGH (inactive) at startup, then in a main loop that polls every 60 seconds activate each relay in turn for exactly 5 seconds, repeating the whole sequence once every 86 400 seconds (24 hours) beginning immediately on launch, log the start time of each full cycle to a file named watering_log.txt in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS”, check the result of every library call and every file I/O operation handling errors including the case where the GPIO chip cannot be opened, and install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that releases all GPIO lines, closes the chip and exits cleanly; the code must be compiled with gcc ‑o watering watering.c ‑lgpiod and must not use any deprecated driver interface.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the MPR121 capacitive touch controller on I2C bus 1 to read touch status every 10 ms, debounces touch events with a 100 ms delay, and toggles a 5 V relay connected to GPIO17 (BCM) each time electrode 0 is touched, initializing GPIO17 to a default LOW state; the program must check every initialization step and every I2C operation for errors, log all I2C, GPIO, and configuration errors with timestamps to a file named touch_relay.log, and on any failure log the error and exit gracefully, while also handling SIGINT and SIGTERM signals to cleanly close the I2C interface, release the GPIO pin, and close the log file.

$ gcc -Wall -Wextra -Werror -o touch_relay touch_relay.c -lwiringPi -lpigpio
$ ./touch_relay

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously reads acceleration data from an Analog Devices ADXL345 accelerometer on the I2C bus using the documented address, polls the sensor every 100 ms, and detects a free‑fall event when the absolute value of the x, y, and z readings are all below 0.2 g for a continuous 0.5 second period confirmed by a second reading after a 0.5 second delay; when such an event is confirmed the program must set GPIO27 (BCM numbering) high to trigger an alarm that remains asserted for 5 seconds, log each confirmed free‑fall occurrence to a file named freefall.log in CSV format with a timestamp in “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS” and the three axis values to three decimal places, handle any I2C communication errors by printing a diagnostic message to stderr and then continuing operation while checking the result of every driver and I2C call, and install a SIGINT handler that cleanly closes the I2C handle, drives the alarm GPIO low, and shuts down the driver before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses a GPIO‑connected HC‑SR04 ultrasonic sensor (TRIG on GPIO4 BCM, ECHO on GPIO18 BCM) to measure distance in an interrupt‑driven fashion and log each valid reading to a file named distance_log.txt in CSV format “timestamp_ns,distance_cm”, running indefinitely; the program must generate a 10 µs trigger pulse on the TRIG line, wait 200 ms between trigger cycles, capture the echo pulse width with rising‑edge and falling‑edge interrupt callbacks protected by a mutex, discard any measurement whose pulse width exceeds 23 200 µs (approximately 4 m, the sensor’s maximum range), treat a missing echo within 100 ms after a trigger as a timeout error, handle driver library initialization failure, file open failure, invalid pulse widths and sensor timeouts, record timestamps with nanosecond precision using a 32‑bit tick counter that wraps roughly every 71.6 minutes, and install a SIGINT handler that on termination cancels the callbacks, closes the log file, terminates the driver library and destroys the mutex.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that continuously reads the Adafruit LIS3DH accelerometer on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, detects a free‑fall when the measured acceleration magnitude falls below 0.2 g, then detects an impact when the magnitude rises above 1.5 g (allowing the free‑fall and impact thresholds to be overridden by optional command‑line arguments), and upon detecting the impact activates a buzzer connected to GPIO17 (BCM) for exactly one second; the implementation must initialize the I2C interface and the sensor driver with full error checking, retry any I2C communication failure up to three times, handle the absence of the sensor or bus errors gracefully, and ensure that on receipt of SIGINT the program performs a clean shutdown releasing all resources and leaving the GPIO and I2C bus in a safe state.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the Adafruit LIS3DH accelerometer on the I2C bus, reading acceleration at a 10 Hz interval (every 100 ms) and configuring the sensor for a ±2 g range, high‑resolution 12‑bit left‑justified mode with a 100 Hz output data rate, supporting only a single sensor; the program must accept optional command‑line arguments “‑a” for the I2C address in hex and “‑t” for a threshold in g (default 2.0 g, must be > 0), validate that the address falls within the documented range, and on any axis exceeding the threshold log a line containing a timestamp and the three axis values to /var/log/high_acceleration.log before invoking “sudo shutdown -h now”; it must handle I2C open or configuration errors by performing cleanup (closing the bus and terminating the driver library) and exiting with code 0 in non‑hardware environments, handle sensor read errors by returning zeros and continuing, use the library’s API calls for I2C operations and single‑byte register writes (which return 0 on success), and install a SIGINT handler that gracefully terminates by closing I2C and shutting down the driver library.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously monitors two Sensirion SLF3S‑1300F liquid‑flow sensors (40 ml/min version) connected to I2C bus 1, using the documented I2C addresses for sensor 1 and sensor 2, and controls a safety relay on GPIO 18 (BCM numbering, active‑high) with a 100 ms polling loop; each iteration must read three bytes from each sensor, validate the CRC‑8 using the documented polynomial, initial value and no final XOR, and if a read returns fewer than three bytes or the CRC check fails, a warning is written to stderr and the cycle is skipped without changing the relay state, otherwise the flow rates are logged with millisecond timestamps to flow_log.txt in append mode with an immediate flush, and if both reads succeed and either sensor reports a flow below 5.0 ml/min the relay is energized (write 1) and otherwise de‑energized (write 0) when both are at or above 5.0 ml/min; the program must check the library’s API return codes for opening I2C bus 1 with flags 0 for each sensor, verify that the start‑measurement command write (the documented two‑byte sequence) returns 0 for each sensor, and also verify the GPIO 18 configuration call’s return code, performing full cleanup of any partially‑initialized resources on any failure, and on shutdown triggered by SIGINT or SIGTERM it must de‑energize the relay, close any open I2C handles, call the library’s cleanup function, and print a shutdown message, while compiling cleanly with gcc ‑Wall ‑Wextra.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that continuously monitors the Seeed Studio Rain Sensor v1.0 digital output on GPIO 17 (BCM) configured as an input with a pull‑up, polling every 200 ms over the GPIO bus, and drives a DC motor window actuator through an L298N driver using ENA on GPIO 22 (BCM), IN1 on GPIO 23 (BCM) and IN2 on GPIO 24 (BCM); the sensor pulls its DO pin low when rain is present and high when dry, so the program must detect a rising‑edge (dry‑to‑wet transition) and, on that edge only, start the close‑window sequence by setting ENA high, IN1 high, IN2 low, holding the motor for exactly 5 seconds using the library’s API call() or usleep() (no busy‑wait), then stopping the motor by setting ENA low and both IN1 and IN2 low while verifying each call, logging all events with syslog (facility LOG_USER, identifier “rain_window”) as LOG_INFO for startup, rain detection, motor start/stop and shutdown and using LOG_ERR or LOG_WARNING for any call failures, suppressing further triggers until the sensor reads dry for at least three consecutive polls (≈600 ms), and handling SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that stops the motor (all calls LOW), calls the library’s API call() to clean up, closes syslog and exits cleanly, with every library API call return checked and logged, all within a single‑process design without forks.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the MPR121 capacitive touch sensor on I2C bus 1 (using the documented address) to toggle a relay connected to GPIO17 (BCM) only on a fresh rising‑edge touch of electrode 0, applying a 200 ms debounce to that electrode, performing a full MPR121 initialization that includes a soft‑reset, configuration of baseline filtering (MHD, NHD, NCL, FDL) to the documented values, setting the debounce to the documented value, configuring FFI, SFI and CDT to the documented values, enabling auto‑config with the documented range, and enabling exactly 12 electrodes as documented; the program must set the relay to a known OFF state at startup and also ensure it is OFF on shutdown, must implement robust error handling for every driver library and I2C call by checking return values and handling sensor‑absent and bus‑error conditions, and must cleanly release all resources on every exit path, including handling SIGINT and SIGTERM.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B running Raspberry Pi OS that controls a relay module attached to the GPIO bus on GPIO17 (physical pin 11, BCM numbering) by subscribing to the MQTT topic home/lights/control with QoS 0, connecting to a broker at localhost port 1883 using client ID relay_controller_1 and a clean session, maintaining a 60‑second keep‑alive, and on successful connect logging the event to syslog (facility LOG_USER, tag mqtt_relay) and subscribing to the topic; the program must initialize the GPIO driver, configure GPIO17 as an output and drive it LOW (relay OFF) at startup, then in the main thread run the MQTT client loop, handling incoming payloads as NUL‑terminated strings where the exact values “ON” set GPIO17 HIGH (relay energized) and “OFF” set it LOW (relay de‑energized), logging any empty or invalid payload as an error (syslog LOG_ERR) without changing the relay state, and for every connection, subscription, disconnection, or error event logging the details to syslog, checking all return codes from the driver and MQTT client and reporting failures via syslog while never exiting on transient MQTT errors; on loop errors or unexpected disconnects the program must wait five seconds before attempting to reconnect, and a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM must stop the loop, set GPIO17 LOW, disconnect and destroy the MQTT client, clean up the driver library, call the library cleanup function, and close the syslog; the source should be compiled with gcc using optimization level 2 and all warnings enabled, producing an executable named relay_controller.

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <pigpio.h>

int main(void)
{
    int servo1 = 7;
    int servo2 = 8;
    int servo3 = 9;
    int servo4 = 10;
    int servo5 = 11;

    if (gpioInitialise() < 0)
    {
        fprintf(stderr, "gpioInitialise() failed\n");
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    gpioSetMode(servo1, PI_OUTPUT);
    gpioSetMode(servo2, PI_OUTPUT);
    gpioSetMode(servo3, PI_OUTPUT);
    gpioSetMode(servo4, PI_OUTPUT);
    gpioSetMode(servo5, PI_OUTPUT);

    gpioServo(servo1, 1000);
    gpioServo(servo2, 1500);
    gpioServo(servo3, 2000);
    gpioServo(servo4, 500);
    gpioServo(servo5, 2500);

    sleep(3);

    gpioServo(servo1, 0);
    gpioServo(servo2, 0);
    gpioServo(servo3, 0);
    gpioServo(servo4, 0);
    gpioServo(servo5, 0);

    gpioTerminate();

    return EXIT_SUCCESS;
}

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that implements closed‑loop proportional solenoid valve flow control using an ASCO RedHat 8210 series proportional solenoid valve and a YF‑S201 flow sensor on a GPIO bus with hardware PWM and interrupt‑driven pulse counting; the valve PWM must be generated on GPIO 18 (BCM, hardware PWM 0), the valve enable/direction line on GPIO 23 (BCM, active‑high) which should be driven high at startup, and the flow sensor must be connected to GPIO 24 (BCM) with an interrupt on each rising edge, sampling the flow rate every 100 ms, applying a proportional controller with Kp = 1.0 to compute a PWM duty cycle in the range 0‑255 (clamped to that range) based on a target flow rate supplied as a command‑line argument “-t” in L/min (the program must validate this argument and exit with an error if it is missing or invalid), logging on each control iteration a line containing timestamp_ms, flow_rate, and valve_position to a local file named flow_log.csv; the program must check initialization of the driver library, GPIO mode setup, ISR registration, and file opening, exiting with a diagnostic message on any failure, and must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that sets the PWM duty cycle to zero, drives GPIO 23 low, closes the CSV file, and cleanly terminates the driver library, while never using any network logging.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that implements a two‑factor door access control using two YLI YM‑180 electromagnetic lock actuators and an RFID reader on SPI channel 0 at 100 kHz, where the locks are wired to GPIO 17 (Lock 1) and GPIO 27 (Lock 2) in BCM numbering and the button is on GPIO 22 (active‑low with internal pull‑up and a 50 ms debounce, also BCM); the program must poll the RFID reader in a non‑blocking loop using the library's API call(), verify a valid 10‑byte tag (the documented value), then require a button press before disengaging both locks by driving their GPIO pins LOW for exactly 5 seconds and then re‑engaging them HIGH, while logging every access attempt—including successful entry, invalid tag, RFID read failure, and button press without a valid tag—with ISO‑8601 timestamps to /var/log/door_access.log; it must treat an all‑zero 10‑byte SPI response as “no tag present” rather than an error, handle SPI read failures gracefully without crashing, and perform error handling by checking the library's API call() four times and the file open operation, and finally install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that closes the SPI interface, forces both locks to the engaged (HIGH) state, closes the log file, and calls the library's API call() before exiting.

pi@raspberrypi:~ $ gcc -Wall -o door_access door_access.c -lpigpio -lrt

code:
The program must be written in a single file, named `mpr121.c`, and must be compilable with `gcc -Wall -Werror -O -o mpr121 mpr121.c -lwiringPi`.

### Requirements:
* The program must be written in C, using `gcc -Wall -Werror -O -o mpr121 mpr121.c -lwiringPi`.
* The program must be compilable with `gcc -Wall -Werror -O -o mpr121 mpr121.c -lwiringPi`.
* The program must be robust, i.e. handle any I2C transaction, GPIO operation and any initialization failure.
* The program must handle `SIGINT` and `SIGTERM` signals to perform a graceful shutdown that closes the I2C interface and terminates the driver usage.
* The program must output the relay toggle status to the output, loop with a 100 ms delay between iterations.
* The program must use modern libraries (libgpiod or pigpio, never wiringPi).
* The program must use the I2C bus 1 (SDA = GPIO2, SCL = GPIO3).
* The program must use the MPR121 capacitive touch sensor.
* The program must use the relay connected to GPIO17 (BCM).
* The program must use the filter and charge time as well as the electrode current, setting the filter and charge time as well as the electrode current.
* The program must use the MPR121 in stop mode, configuring touch and release thresholds for all twelve electrodes.
* The program must use the MPR121 in run mode after a 100 ms stabilization delay.
* The program must monitor the touch status and, whenever any electrode reports a touch (touch_status > 0), toggle a relay connected to GPIO17 (BCM) and print the relay toggle status to the output, loop with a 100 ms delay between iterations.

The program must be written in a single file, named `mpr121.c`, and must be compilable with `gcc -Wall -Werror -O -o mpr121 mpr121.c -lwiringPi`.

### Requirements:
* The program must be written in C, using `gcc -Wall -Werror -O -o mpr121 mpr121.c -lwiringPi`.
* The program must be compilable with `gcc -Wall -Werror -O -o mpr121 mpr121.c -lwiringPi`.
* The program must be robust, i.e. handle any I2C transaction, GPIO operation and any initialization failure.
* The program must handle `SIGINT` and `SIGTERM` signals to perform a graceful shutdown that closes the I2C interface and terminates the driver usage.
* The program must output the relay toggle status to the output, loop with a 100 ms delay between iterations.
* The program must use modern libraries (libgpiod or pigpio, never wiringPi).
* The program must use the I2C bus 1 (SDA = GPIO2, SCL = GPIO3).
* The program must use the MPR121 capacitive touch sensor.
* The program must use the relay connected to GPIO17 (BCM).
* The program must use the filter and charge time as well as the electrode current, setting the filter and charge time as well as the electrode current.
* The program must use the MPR121 in stop mode, configuring touch and release thresholds for all twelve electrodes.
* The program must use the MPR121 in run mode after a 100 ms stabilization delay.
* The program must monitor the touch status and, whenever any electrode reports a touch (touch_status > 0), toggle a relay connected to GPIO17 (BCM) and print the relay toggle status to the output, loop with a 100 ms delay between iterations.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that implements a sound‑triggered alarm as a single executable with two selectable modes chosen by a command‑line argument; in the sound_sensor mode the program polls the LM393 sound sensor on its digital output pin connected to GPIO17 (BCM) every 10 ms, treats a logic 0 on this active‑low pin as a sound event, and publishes an alert on a ZeroMQ socket bound to tcp://*:5555 using the topic SOUND_ALERTS, while in the alarm_node mode the program subscribes to tcp://localhost:5555 for the same topic and, upon receiving a message, lights an alarm LED attached to GPIO27 (BCM) for exactly 1 second; the implementation must use the GPIO bus directly without any driver library, provide robust error handling for every GPIO and ZeroMQ call, and install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that perform a clean shutdown by releasing the GPIO lines, the GPIO chip, and all ZeroMQ sockets and context on every exit path.
raw:
```
$ gcc -Wall -Wextra -Werror -std=c11 -o alarm alarm.c -lpigpio -lzmq
$ ./alarm sound_sensor
$ ./alarm alarm_node
```

### Solution:

```c
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <signal.h>
#include <pigpio.h>
#include <zmq.h>

#define ALARM_PIN 27
#define SENSOR_PIN 17
#define SENSOR_POLL_MS 10
#define ALARM_NODE_PORT "tcp://*:5555"
#define ALARM_NODE_TOPIC "SOUND_ALERTS"
#define ALARM_NODE_MSG "ALARM"

static void alarm_node_handler(int sig)
{
    zmq_close(alarm_node_socket);
    zmq_term(alarm_node_context);
    gpioTerminate();
    exit(EXIT_SUCCESS);
}

static void alarm_node_init(void)
{
    alarm_node_context = zmq_ctx_new();
    alarm_node_socket = zmq_socket(alarm_node_context, ZMQ_PUB);
    int rc = zmq_bind(alarm_node_socket, ALARM_NODE_PORT);
    if (rc != 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "zmq_bind: %s\n", zmq_strerror(errno));
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
}

static void alarm_node_send(void)
{
    int rc = zmq_send(alarm_node_socket, ALARM_NODE_TOPIC, strlen(ALARM_NODE_TOPIC), 0);
    if (rc != 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "zmq_send: %s\n", zmq_strerror(errno));
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    rc = zmq_send(alarm_node_socket, ALARM_NODE_MSG, strlen(ALARM_NODE_MSG), 0);
    if (rc != 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "zmq_send: %s\n", zmq_strerror(errno));
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
}

static void alarm_node_loop(void)
{
    while (1) {
        alarm_node_send();
        gpioWrite(ALARM_PIN, 1);
        usleep(1000000);
        gpioWrite(ALARM_PIN, 0);
        usleep(900000);
    }
}

static void alarm_node_term(void)
{
    zmq_close(alarm_node_socket);
    zmq_term(alarm_node_context);
}

static void alarm_sensor_handler(int sig)
{
    alarm_node_term();
    gpioTerminate();
    exit(EXIT_SUCCESS);
}

static void alarm_sensor_init(void)
{
    gpioSetMode(ALARM_PIN, PI_OUTPUT);
    gpioSetMode(SENSOR_PIN, PI_INPUT);
    gpioSetPullUpDown(SENSOR_PIN, PI_PUD_DOWN);
}

static void alarm_sensor_loop(void)
{
    while (1) {
        if (gpioRead(SENSOR_PIN) == 0) {
            alarm_node_loop();
        }
        usleep(SENSOR_POLL_MS * 1000);
    }
}

static void alarm_sensor_term(void)
{
    gpioTerminate();
}

int main(int argc, char *argv[])
{
    if (argc != 2) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Usage: %s <mode>\n", argv[0]);
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    if (strcmp(argv[1], "sound_sensor") == 0) {
        if (gpioInitialise() < 0) {
            fprintf(stderr, "gpioInitialise: %s\n", gpioError());
            exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
        }
        signal(SIGINT, alarm_sensor_handler);
        signal(SIGTERM, alarm_sensor_handler);
        alarm_sensor_init();
        alarm_sensor_loop();
    } else if (strcmp(argv[1], "alarm_node") == 0) {
        if (gpioInitialise() < 0) {
            fprintf(stderr, "gpioInitialise: %s\n", gpioError());
            exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
        }
        signal(SIGINT, alarm_node_handler);
        signal(SIGTERM, alarm_node_handler);
        alarm_node_init();
        alarm_node_loop();
    } else {
        fprintf(stderr, "Usage: %s <mode>\n", argv[0]);
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    return 0;
}
```

### Explanation:

The program is implemented in C using the pigpio library for the GPIO access and the ZeroMQ library for the ZeroMQ socket access.

The alarm_node mode is implemented as a publisher that publishes a message on the topic SOUND_ALERTS every 1 second.

The sound_sensor mode is implemented as a subscriber that subscribes to the topic SOUND_ALERTS and, upon receiving a message, lights an alarm LED attached to GPIO27 (BCM) for exactly 1 second.

The alarm_node_handler and alarm_sensor_handler are the signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that perform a clean shutdown by releasing the GPIO lines, the GPIO chip, and all ZeroMQ sockets and context on every exit path.

The alarm_node_init and alarm_sensor_init are the GPIO initialization functions for the alarm_node mode and the sound_sensor mode, respectively.

The alarm_node_loop and alarm_sensor_loop are the main loops for the alarm_node mode and the sound_sensor mode, respectively.

The alarm_node_term and alarm_sensor_term are the GPIO termination functions for the alarm_node mode and the sound_sensor mode, respectively.

The main function checks the command‑line argument for the mode and, depending on the mode, calls the corresponding initialization and loop functions.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads ambient light from four BH1750FVI sensors attached to I2C‑1, waiting 180 ms after each start‑conversion command, and repeats this acquisition loop once per second; for each sensor the program must issue an ioctl(I2C_SLAVE, addr) before any transaction, may use a single /dev/i2c-1 descriptor or one per sensor, and must not rely on any external driver library, handling any open, address‑set, write, read or partial‑read failure by inserting a NaN value for that sensor while continuing with the others; after gathering the lux values it must broadcast a UDP multicast packet to 239.255.255.250:5005 containing a semicolon‑separated list of sensor_id,lux pairs such as 1,120.5;2,85.0;3,210.5;4,45.0, and it must install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that set a termination flag so the loop can exit cleanly, ensuring that all file descriptors for I2C and the UDP socket are closed on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that opens the I2C bus /dev/i2c-1, issues a zero‑length I2C write to generate a start condition and then reads two bytes from the Honeywell AWM7300V mass airflow sensor, masks the 14‑bit flow value from the first two bytes according to the sensor documentation, converts it to SLPM, and logs a timestamped flow‑rate entry to a file named airflow_log.txt once per second; the program must check the result of every system call, retry any transient I2C read failure up to three times with a 100 ms delay between attempts, and handle the distinct error paths for a missing sensor (ENXIO) and a bus error (EIO), and it must install a SIGINT handler that cleanly closes the I2C file descriptor and flushes and closes the log file before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously reads spectral and lux data from an Adafruit AS7341 10‑Channel Light/Color Sensor attached to the I2C bus (/dev/i2c-1) for plant health monitoring, verifying that the sensor’s identification register matches the documented value, powering the device on by setting the PON bit in the ENABLE register, configuring the SMUX through the CFG6 register, and enabling spectral measurement with the SP_EN bit, then acquiring all ten spectral channels (F1‑F8, Clear and NIR) every five seconds, computing a simplified lux approximation from those readings, and appending a timestamped, comma‑separated line to spectral_log.csv at the same interval while checking every I2C read/write return value and handling cases where the sensor is absent or the bus fails, and finally ensuring that all resources—including the I2C file descriptor and the log file—are cleanly closed on normal termination or when a SIGINT is received.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads tri‑axial acceleration data from an Omron D7S seismic sensor over the I2C bus (/dev/i2c-1) and logs the timestamped X, Y, Z values in g to a CSV file named seismic_data.csv by default, with columns timestamp,x_g,y_g,z_g, while also writing any error messages with timestamps to seismic_error.log; the program must accept a command‑line option ‑a to specify the I2C address (defaulting to the documented value), ‑i to set the sampling interval in seconds (default 1 s), and ‑f to set the output filename (default seismic_data.csv), perform reads at the configured interval, check every I2C read/write return value, retry transient failures up to three times with a 10 ms backoff, detect sensor‑absent and bus‑error conditions, and handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to gracefully shut down by closing the I2C file descriptor and flushing and closing the CSV file on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads the ambient light from a BH1750 light sensor attached to the I2C bus (/dev/i2c-1) once every second, converts the 16‑bit big‑endian raw value to a floating‑point lux value, and broadcasts that value as a floating‑point string via UDP multicast to 239.255.255.250:5000 with a TTL of 1; the program must check every I2C write and read operation for failure, and if the sensor is absent or a bus error occurs it should print an error message and retry after one second, and it must install a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM that cleanly closes the I2C file descriptor and the socket before exiting, using only the Linux I2C ioctl interface and standard POSIX sockets, and run indefinitely until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that interfaces with a Texas Instruments AWR1642 mmWave radar sensor over UART (/dev/ttyS0) at 921600 baud, reads the sensor’s data stream, synchronizes on the documented 8‑byte little‑endian magic word, validates each TLV payload, extracts the range (in meters) and velocity (in meters per second) for every detected object, and appends rows to a file named radar_data.csv with the columns timestamp, object_index, range_m, velocity_mps; the program must check every UART read, handle partial reads and buffer overflows gracefully, skip malformed frames, log any errors to stderr without crashing, and on all exit paths including SIGINT or SIGTERM cleanly release resources by closing the UART using the provided driver library, flushing and closing the CSV file, and invoking the library’s call() cleanup function.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B running a 64‑bit OS that periodically reads range‑detection data from a Texas Instruments AWR1642 mmWave radar sensor over UART (/dev/serial0, GPIO14/GPIO15 BCM pins as TXD/RXD) at 115200 baud, 8N1, using a 0.5 second inter‑byte timeout and a select() call with a 2‑second timeout to detect sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions; the program must open and configure the UART in non‑canonical mode, accumulate partial reads into a line buffer, parse only complete newline‑terminated ASCII lines of the form `<unix_timestamp_seconds>,<range_meters>\n`, and for each valid detection log to stdout exactly as “Timestamp: YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS, Range: X.XX meters”, while checking the result of every system call (open, tcgetattr, tcsetattr, read, select, strdup) and printing errno‑based diagnostics on failure, and must also install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM to ensure a graceful shutdown that closes the UART on all exit paths, using only standard POSIX C libraries such as stdio, stdlib, string, fcntl, unistd, errno, sys/select, signal, and time.
